items.title: Why do we even do inheritance?
items.content_html:
Why do we even do inheritance? Why do your kids get a right to your shit when you're dead? Those kids never had to do a damn thing for it and yet they get it anyway. And if you want to support your kid financially so badly, just do that while you're still alive.

It's just rich people staying rich for no reason. Your kid didn't do anything. They were just born to the right parents, and now they get a free house or a pile of money for it. That's not fair, that's just luck.

As far as I'm concerned we should just abolish the whole inheritance system. And just think about the advantages of that:

  • A ton of houses would become available, because they wouldn't stay stuck in families anymore but would just go on the market
  • We'd shrink wealth inequality and opportunity inequality
  • All the money you have left over could go straight to the tax office, and then we could actually do so many nice things with it that everyone benefits from
  • Rich families would actually have to stay rich by doing something, instead of just waiting for grandpa to die

And before anyone starts: no, I'm not saying you have to sell your grandma's ring or her photo albums, stuff that actually has sentimental value you can just keep. I'm talking about the million-euro house and the 300k sitting in some account that you're about to inherit.

By the way, hii to all the VVD voters reading this, you're probably sitting super mad in your own house right now (paid for with money you got from an inheritance), but I'd love to remind you that liberal economics makes a very clear difference between earned income (where you actually did something) and unearned income, and unless you commit murder, your parents dying isn't something you had to do anything for

items.title: Euro banknotes are getting a redesign and I have opinions
items.content_html:
The European Central Bank (BCE/ECB/ЕЦБ/EZB/EKP/EKT/ESB/EKB/BĊE/EBC) is redesigning the euro banknotes. After years of committees and surveys, we've finally reached the fun part: 10 designs made the shortlist, and they went public this month.

The old notes

The first euro banknote series was made by Austrian designer Robert Kalina in 2002. It's built around windows, doorways, and bridges, but none of them are real buildings.

After that came the "Europa series", a redesign of the first one by designer Reinhold Gerstetter.

Why?

The Europa series still does its job, so why? The ECB gives a few reasons.

The boring-but-important one is counterfeiting: reproduction tech keeps getting better, so every so often the notes need fresh security features to stay ahead. A full redesign is a good excuse to add those./And they say the new notes will also be more accessible, especially for people who are visually impaired. They want to make them more durable and more sustainable too.

Two new themes

After many surveys, the ECB picked 2 themes: "European culture" and "Rivers and birds" for the new notes. Here's how the ECB describes them:

  • "European culture: Europe's rich cultural heritage and dynamic cultural and creative sectors strengthen the European identity, forging a shared sense of belonging. Culture promotes common values, inclusion and dialogue in Europe and across the globe. It brings people together."
  • "Rivers and birds: Rivers and birds recognise no borders, symbolising freedom and unity amongst Europeans and our connection to nature. Europe boasts a wide variety of rivers and birds that inspire us and remind us of our responsibility to protect the environment."

Each note gets its own motifs depending on the theme:

European culture

The front shows a famous European, and the back shows a scene that matches that note's theme.

Note Person Theme
€5 Maria Callas Performing arts
€10 Ludwig van Beethoven Music
€20 Marie Curie (born Skłodowska) Universities and schools
€50 Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra Libraries
€100 Leonardo da Vinci Museums and exhibitions
€200 Bertha von Suttner Public squares

Rivers and birds

Here the front shows a landscape and a bird, and the back shows an EU institution.

Note Landscape Bird Building
€5 Mountain spring Wallcreeper European Parliament
€10 Waterfall Kingfisher European Commission
€20 River valley Bee-eater colony European Central Bank
€50 Meandering river White stork Court of Justice of the European Union
€100 River mouth Avocet European Council and Council of the European Union
€200 Seascape Northern gannet European Court of Auditors

The shortlist

Getting from 2 themes to 10 designs took a while. Over 1,200 designers and studios across the EU applied, 25 were asked to make full proposals, and a jury of 21 independent experts picked the 10 you see below. The ECB has a public survey open until 21 September 2026, and at the end of the year, they will make a descision

Side note:everything below is just my opinion. I'm not an amazing designer, I've got no special expertise here, I just really like this stuff and have thoughts. So (after reading this) go look at the designs yourself and make up your own mind. (And then go vote!)

Design A by Studio Joost Grootens

The notes are fine, but that's about it for me. The rest falls a bit flat: the fronts feel empty, the portraits aren't visually really appealing, and those silhouette figures are just weird. This gives me school textbook vibes, not money.

Design B by PunktFormStrich

Wow, okay, these are gorgeous. Design A stuck to one main colour with a secondary accent, but this one really uses each note's colour amazingly. The buildings look great, and you can directly tell that the river landscapes are actually rivers. My favourite bit are the little details under the birds, it's genuinely fun to read (it's in English though, I would have have liked something language-neutral). These feel like notes that could really exist. Just beautiful.

Design C by Neue Gestaltung GmbH

Someone please remind them this was meant to be a banknote, not a company report. The left and right bits are okay (the portraits are a bit dull, but the little constellations on the map of Europe are cool), but the middle ruins it. You can just about tell what it's supposed to be, a piano, a chemistry set, some books, but it looks so, so corporate. Way more like the cover of a company report than money.

Design D by Rudy Guedj and François Girard-Meunier

Okay, this one is on another level. Design B still left some white space along the sides, but here the notes are filled with colour from edge to edge, and it works so well. I absolutely love this. The details ARE SO GOOD: the actual waveform of a bird call, tiny footprints of the birds, a feather, more bird-sound stuff, IT'S SO GOOD. The backs are about as European as it gets too (I don't get the hands though). The 10 and 50 notes look a bit too alik tough. But overall, just really, really good.

Design E by Myrsini Vardopoulou

These feel washed out to me. Flat, lifeless, really like pale colours, kind of boring. And because everything is so muted, the notes are hard to tell apart, which doesn't help. Not terrible, but far from great.

Design F by Jan Robert Dünnweller

Gorgeous, honestly so beautifully drawn. But well... it isn't really money. Each note is an amazing bit of art, really nicely done, and yet I just can't picture handing one over at a shop. Beautiful, just not quite money.

Design G by Rubio & del Amo and Cruz más Cruz

Pretty sure the brief was money for the Eurozone, not Monopoly. It all feels too busy and too playful for real currency. That said, it's nicely designed, and these are the coolest portraits on the whole list. But like design C, the art style is so corporate.

Design H by Atelier Goppel-Toperngpong

Fantastic. Honestly so, so beautiful. The buildings are gorgeous, the colours are lovely, and these are by far the nicest birds on the whole shortlist. It looks a lot like the current notes, but in a good way. It feels familiar and fresh at the same time, and out of all ten this is the one I can most easily picture actually becoming real money. It could maybe use a bit more of that "Europe" feeling somewhere, but otherwise just gorgeous.

Design I by Isabelle Daëron

A bit boring, nothing too special here. They look more like a set of Pokemon cards than banknotes. And it doesn't feel very creative either: it's like they followed the assignment to the letter and then just did nothing, not adding anything creative.

Design J by Ville Tietäväinen

Pretty similar to design I, but a bit better. I really like the buildings shown as silhouettes inside the wings, and the birds have a cool style, even if they look more like a comic than a banknote. The little figures along the bottom of the backs add to that comic feel too. Not bad, just not really money again.

So, which one?

Design D and design H are my clear favourites, with design B close behind them, all beautiful and the ones that feel most like real, usable money.

Two more things

I think rivers and birds is a much better theme than European culture. With European culture you're guaranteed to disappoint someone: it's so big and so diverse that whoever you pick to put on a note, you're leaving out a hundred other things that deserved a spot just as much. There is a reason the current notes use fictional bridges and not real ones. Rivers and birds gives designers a lot more to play with, and it's way more universal too.

I'm also not a fan of the fully vertical notes (design G, I, and J). That's just not how people hold banknotes, and it makes them look like they were made for your phone screen instead of your wallet.

Go vote

A big thanks to everyone behind these 10 designs. Even the ones I didn't like had a ton of work and care put into them, so big love to all of you.

If you've got opinions too (and after all this, how could you not), go fill in the ECB's survey before 21 September 2026 and let them know what you think.

items.title: On school phone bans
items.content_html:
Pretty much all Dutch schools already have a phone ban or are considering one. And I think this is unfair.

Let me first say, I completely agree that phones do not belong in classrooms during lessons. They are distracting and addictive, and they take away your focus during the lesson. Banning phones during lessons is completely fair and understandable.

But what most Dutch schools are doing is an outright ban on phones in the entire school building, which is indefensible in my opinion. Why would you not be allowed to have your phone in the hallway or during breaks? It's not like you're learning less just because you're looking at a screen instead of the floor while walking through school.

And what exactly is the point of banning phones during tussenuren? What goal are you even trying to achieve? There's no lesson being disrupted, and nobody is losing focus. Students just have a free period and nothing to do, and Dutch schools can have A LOT of tussenuren. You're just taking something away for no reason whatsoever.

Oh and if we're doing this, it should apply to everyone equally. Teachers, support staff, the janitor, the secretary, everyone. You cannot tell students they can't have their phones while teachers and staff walk around with theirs all day. And I can already hear the teachers say, "Oh but what if there is an emergency and I need to be called?" LIKE STUDENTS DON'T HAVE EMERGENCIES WHEN THEY SHOULD BE CALLED? "Oh yes no but it is essential for me to access the attendance system." WELL IT IS ALSO ESSENTIAL FOR US TO CHECK OUR SCHEDULE WHICH IS IN THE SAME DAMN SYSTEM.

Also, education has a big role in preparing children for society, and I hate to break it to you, but everyone in society uses mobile phones all the time. So it is way better to teach the children how to use their phones wisely and warn them about the dangers instead of just banning phones altogether. And spoiler: in higher education, phones are just allowed too. So you're not preparing us for society, and you're not even preparing us for the next step in our education. Great job.

On top of that, you cannot make all of our education systems digital and then take away our phones. I am absolutely outraged when I hear an adult (most often teachers) being angry at the fact that students are "all looking at their phones when walking between lessons" WHEN THOSE VERY TEACHERS ARE THE ONES THAT SET UP SYSTEMS WHERE THE ONLY PLACE WE CAN SEE OUR SCHEDULE IS OUR PHONE. YOU CANNOT MAKE US DEPEND ON OUR PHONES FOR SCHOOL AND THEN GET ANGRY WHEN WE USE THEM.

Completely banning phones in the entire school is total overkill, and it can hurt people too. There are quite a few people without any friends or anyone to talk to during breaks, who use their phones to distract themselves by watching a movie or listening to music. Oh, I don't know if you have realised this yet, but this also means that they're practically banning listening to music in school, which is completely ridiculous.

And if you're genuinely worried about phone use, there are so many better things you could do. Add more activities during breaks and tussenuren. Give students something to actually do. Make the school day more engaging. Put that energy into actually fixing things instead of just taking something away.

Oh and maybe, if students are spending entire lessons on their phones instead of paying attention, maybe the lesson just isn't interesting enough. Maybe the education itself is the problem.

The moment a school starts banning phones in hallways and during tussenuren, they've stopped caring about education and started caring about creating an authoritarian, control-obsessed environment. And we're just supposed to accept that.

items.title: Dear boomers
items.content_html:
Dear boomers, elders, fossils, and other 20th-century people,

I have some bad news: it is not "the past" anymore. I know that can be uncomfortable, especially since many of you remember the past as something better, and use it as a reference point where everything today looks worse by comparison.

But there is worse news: it will not become the past again. Not because anyone is refusing to go back, but because the past isn't a place we can return to. It was a specific combination of people, knowledge, technology, economics, and social norms that no longer exists. The world changed. Quite a lot, actually.

What used to be possible is not automatically a valid benchmark for what should be expected now.

You often use arguments like "you could just do X back then" or "that wasn't a problem before" as criticism of younger generations. But those aren't really arguments about the present. They're comparisons with a different world, under different conditions, with different rules.

Saying "I bought a house at 24" is not economic analysis. Saying "I didn't need a phone all day at school" is not an argument that phones are unnecessary for students (in fact, they are quite necessary every single day for every single student, thanks to the systems you and your generation set up). These are personal anecdotes from a world that no longer exists.

Having lived through earlier versions of society gives perspective, but it does not make that perspective applicable today. The fact that you were young once does not make you an expert on today's youth any more than owning a steam train makes you an expert on modern urban rail systems.

You are absolutely allowed to dislike the changes, criticise them, or even try to fix what went wrong. But it only works if you start from the recognition that everything has changed.

Kind regards,
The present

items.title: My proposal for the Dutch national exam design
items.content_html:
This is a follow-up to my post about the new Dutch exam design

Instead of just complaining, I decided to design something better. My proposal borrows heavily from the old design, because I still think the 2025 layout gets most things right. But it also fixes a few things that were already slightly off before the CvTE made them worse.

The cover

The cover has a lot to communicate: the subject, the school level, the year, the tijdvak (which sitting of the exam it is, because there are multiple each year), the date and time, and which document you're holding. For the exercise booklet specifically, it also shows the number of questions and the maximum score.

Not all of that is equally important. When you pick up the booklet, the first thing you need to know is what you are holding. Subject, year, and document type need to be immediately obvious. Date and time matter much less. So in my design, those three key pieces are the largest and boldest, and everything secondary is smaller and quieter.

I also removed the code in the bottom-left corner that appears on current exams. That code is for administrative use and no student has ever needed it. I replaced it with something actually useful: a clear description of the document and exam.

The rest of the exam

The body of the exam stays close to the old design. Black text on a white background, no decorative shapes, no grey boxes, no icons. This isn't a stylistic preference: it's just the simplest and least distracting choice, which is what you want when you're asking people to read for up to 3 hours.

I dropped the word "Vraag" before every question number, because it adds no information. Everyone already knows what a question number is (and if you don't, you probably shouldn't be setting exams).

Point values are back in front of the question number, where they were in the old design. That makes it easy to scan down a page and understand how points are distributed at a glance. Small thing, but it matters when you're planning your time.

The old design wasn't exciting, but it was clear. Most of the problems with the new CvTE design come from optimising for the wrong thing: making the exam look more modern rather than making it easier to use. If you walked out of the exam hall thinking about question 3 and not the awful booklet, the design has done its job.

You can view the full design as a PDF: exercise booklet and texts booklet.

items.title: The new Dutch exam design is worse
items.content_html:
The Dutch national exams are getting redesigned. The Board for Tests and Examinations (CvTE) has been running pilots since 2025, starting with the Spanish exam for havo. This year even more exams use the new layout, including the English exam for vwo, which I took.

The current design has been around since 2007, so a refresh makes sense. The CvTE says the main driver is new accessibility regulations. But having taken the new exam myself, I don't think it's an improvement at all.

For those unfamiliar with Dutch national exams: the design is pretty plain. No fancy shapes, just black 11pt Arial with the occasional grey border. You can see the 2025 English vwo exam for reference.

Honestly, this design is fine. There's room for improvement (the line-height is a bit tight, and the cover is not always clear), but it does its job. Everything that needs to be communicated is communicated, clearly and without any distractions.

That's what exam design should do. The goal isn't to look good or feel modern: it's to get information across as clearly as possible to as many candidates as possible. A good exam design goes completely unnoticed.

So when you compare the old design to the new one, the problems become obvious pretty quickly.

The new design is full of visual clutter. There are decorative diagonal shapes on the cover, text with weird borders snaking around it, icons, text blocks with grey backgrounds, grey text all over the place, and the word "Vraag" printed in front of every single question number. None of this adds information. It just adds noise, which is exactly what you don't want when someone is trying to concentrate.

The accessibility argument is also hard to take seriously when you look at the grey background blocks they've introduced. Those blocks actually have worse contrast than anything in the old design. For some of the blocks, the contrast ratio is 6.89:1, which actually fails WCAG AAA. The old design, boring as it was, had black text on white paper.

Then there's the bold text problem. In the new design, all questions are printed in bold. The idea is probably to make the questions stand out from the text surrounding them. But questions sometimes need emphasis within them too, and the way the CvTE solved that was to make that text even bolder. In practice, the difference is almost invisible. My English teacher pointed this out to me after the exam. I hadn't noticed it while actually sitting the test (which is exactly the problem).

And then there's the points. In the old design, the number of points for each question was shown before the question number, so you could easily look at a page and immediately get a sense of how the points were distributed across questions. In the new design, the points are in parentheses after the question. Scanning a page to plan your time is now noticeably harder.

What frustrates me most is the irony of it all. The CvTE redesigned these exams specifically for accessibility reasons, and in doing so introduced contrast failures, invisible emphasis, and a more cluttered layout. The old design wasn't exciting, but it was legible. That used to be enough.

items.title: Internalised compliance
items.content_html:
As a student, you get so used to the idea that things just happen to you. Decisions get made somewhere above your head, and your role is basically just to read the email (and sigh a little) and move on. And I pretty much stopped considering that there could be another option.

So being on a committee with teachers has been really weird in a good way. I keep having these moments where someone proposes something and my first instinct is still just "okay, guess that's decided then", but then someone else actually questions it. Or I question it. And instead of getting shut down immediately, there's an actual discussion. Even the big bosses listen. And things change.

It's strange realising that I don't have to just passively absorb every decision that comes down from above. We can push back a little. We can say, "No, we'd rather handle it this way instead."

I didn't realise how deeply I internalised the idea that students are mostly there to comply until I was suddenly in a position where my opinion was expected rather than merely tolerated.

We should definitely listen to students more.

items.title: What is art?
items.content_html:
Defining what art is isn't easy. According to the dictionary on my desk, art is "the result of the ability to creatively express emotions and thoughts".

But that definition raises some questions. If you remove all traces of an artist from an artwork, is it still art? If you paint a canvas completely white, is that art? Is 4 minutes and 33 seconds of silence art? Is this blog art? Is simply everything humans create art, since you can't really make something without thinking about it?

If you say that "being art" isn't binary but more like a spectrum, you'd probably say that minimalistic and simple works are less art-ish, and big, detailed works are more art-ish. But does that mean 20 hours of white noise is more art-ish than 4 minutes and 33 seconds of silence? Does that mean a 10-hour and 7-minute movie of paint drying is less art-ish than a simple cartoon? If you judge how art-ish something is based only on how much "information" it contains, you completely dismiss the story behind the artwork.

So I think you can't call something art just by observing it. You need to know the background, who made it, how it was made, and why it was made, so you can interpret the emotions it is trying to convey.

If you know that the 607-minute-long film about paint drying is a protest against censorship and the unfair costs facing independent filmmakers, then I think it's far more art-ish than a simple cartoon made for children. If you understand that an artwork represents emotions and thoughts, then it becomes meaningful. Context is everything.

And this is where it gets interesting. Take that banana duct-taped to a wall that everyone loves to mock. People dismiss it as "not real art" because it's just a banana. But maybe they're missing the point entirely.

What if that banana actually does make you think? What if it forces you to question why we assign value to objects, why we create hierarchies of "high" and "low" culture, why we need things to be permanent and precious to matter? What if the absurdity is exactly the point: that in our desperation to categorise and commodify everything, we've lost sight of what actually makes us reflect on the world around us?

The problem isn't that "anything can be art". The problem is that people think there should be gatekeepers deciding what counts. They want someone else to tell them what's meaningful so they don't have to do the extremely hard work of thinking for themselves.

And this brings us to an even bigger problem: how schools completely miss the point of art education.

School ruins art

From my experience, art class in school is where they teach what counts as "real art". Instead of encouraging students to find meaning in their own experiences and explore what art can be, schools restrict that exploration. Classical music is "sophisticated", but the song that made you cry at 3 AM isn't worth discussing. Oil paintings are "serious art", but that meme you and your friends laugh at is just "internet culture".

The worst part? Schools teach students that there are "correct" interpretations of artworks. It feels like they have the "right" interpretation of every artwork ever made, and theirs is the only correct one. No room for personal interpretation, no space for students to find their own meaning in the chaos. No consideration that maybe this painting speaks to your feelings or thoughts. School treats art as if every artwork can be reduced to a few principles you're supposed to memorise.

Actual meaning

So what is art, really? I personally think art is anything that creates genuine meaning in the realm of intention and interpretation. It doesn't matter if it's a Renaissance building or a niche shoegaze track. If it makes you think or feel something real, then it's functioning as art.

Art forces us to confront the fundamentals of being human. Why do we feel the need to create? Why do some patterns of sound or colour move us to tears, while others don't affect us at all? Why do we desperately want to share our inner experiences with others, even though we can never truly know if they understand?

These questions don't have answers, and that's exactly what makes them worth asking.

items.title: Education was bad; AI made it worse
items.content_html:
AI can be an awesome tool for writing. I use it myself more often than I like to admit, and it is used a lot in my school.

And that's a problem. School should be about teaching people important knowledge and skills, and maybe even more importantly, it should get people excited about learning. But if students just use AI to do their assignments, school clearly fails at that. And I completely understand that schools need to do something "against" using AI. But schools can't seem to do this right.

My school just takes away our ability to use AI. For writing assignments, we work on a restricted Chromebook or just on paper. And this approach is wrong: it doesn't just block access to AI. It also limits our ability to do research and fully engage with the learning process. Until this year, we could just do research on the Chromebooks, but this is now not possible during writing assignments. This kind of restriction turns education into something even more bureaucratic, tedious, and frustrating, which only pushes students further away from learning and makes them more likely to rely on AI.

What schools ideally want is that their students don't want to use AI. The experience of learning new things should be engaging and exciting. But that is not the case, and it wasn't the case before AI.

And the students aren't the problem: the endless obsession with assignments, tests, and just accomplishing results is. These assignments, like the project from civics and the writing assignment from NLT, don't let students think about the subject. They just let the students answer some predefined questions, only to get some grade or result.

And AI has removed all room to be curious (there wasn't much room before anyway). My school thinks that if you allow people to be curious, you allow them to use AI.

The endless amount of boring, tedious, and repetitive assignments makes people forget that school can be fun. So for almost everyone, learning is not an interesting experience: it's a chore, so it's no wonder they would rather let AI do it.

items.title: The Dutch Government is ruining its election system
items.content_html:
The Dutch Minister of the Interior and Kingdom Relations Judith Uitermark (NSC) recently announced her plan to transform the Dutch election system by introducing a new system where 125 of the 150 members of the Second Chamber (the most important parliament in the Netherlands) would be elected via regional elections.[1] Her justification? It's to "strengthen the regional bond between voters and elected officials." What a load of nonsense. Let's be clear: this is a step in the wrong direction, and it's a move that will ultimately weaken Dutch democracy itself.

Let's break this down. The election for the Second Chamber is supposed to be a national election, not a regional one. We already have regional elections: the Provincial Council elections (Provinciale Statenverkiezingen). So, if there's an issue with regional representation, why on earth would you mess with the national system? If regional representation is flawed, FIX THE REGIONAL SYSTEM. Don't mess with the national one. Once again, the elections for the Second Chamber are national elections, so everyone in the entire country should be able to vote for the same candidates on their ballot. Otherwise, it's just a bunch of completely separate regional elections which happen to be added up for one parliament. How can you justify a NATIONAL election where your ballot differs depending on where you live?

But that's just the start of the problems. Smaller parties will have their votes scattered across multiple districts, making it much harder for them to secure any seats at all. These parties, which rely on proportional representation, will see their votes effectively wasted.[2] What's the point of voting if your vote doesn't even count? This is the kind of thing we see in places like the United States, where if you don't vote for one of the two main parties, you might as well not vote at all. That is not democracy.

Think about it: systems where votes are effectively lost, like in the U.S., or where a party can get a minority of the votes, but a majority of seats in Parliament, like in the UK, are systems that can generate simply undemocratic outcomes. And now, the Dutch government is trying to take us down that very same path.

It's time to stop this before it's too late. I truly hope the Second Chamber, or the First Chamber, or hell, even the Raad van State steps in to block this plan. At this point, I don't care where it comes from. Just stop it. We cannot allow the Dutch election system to be ruined like this. We cannot allow the Dutch government to just abolish this core democratic principle.

References

  1. Minister wil verkiezingen drastisch veranderen: Tweede Kamerleden per provincie gekozen - RTL Nieuws
  2. NSC's electoral reform plan may have unwanted consequences - University of Groningen

items.title: Introduction
items.content_html:
Hello there! Welcome to this "blog" :D

But that word "blog" doesn't tell you much about what you can expect to find on this "frequently updated website"[1]. "blog" is a word without that much actual meaning to it. Is a blog a place to talk about your latest projects? Is a blog a place to reflect on what you have achieved (like an NLT-logboek)? Is a blog a collection of stories from a road trip through Western Senegal? Is a blog a place to rant about politics? Is a blog just an old place where people wrote things before Twitter existed? Is a blog a place to showcase your work and impress others? Should a blog be made out of lengthy essays with fancy references, or should it be made out of short messages about anything that is on someone's mind?

I think a blog can be all of those, and it definitely shouldn't be a precisely defined thing, and that is amazing.

And I do not know the purpose of this blog. I just wanted to write some things, and I wanted a little place on the internet to store and show them, so here I am.

This is probably the worst welcome post in existence.

References

  1. Blog in the Oxford English Dictionary
